reason: The sources provide over 20 well-documented and cross-referenced claims about Sputnik 1's design, launch, and global cultural impact.
story: On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a polished metal sphere the size of a beach ball. This 'fellow traveler' shocked the United States, sparking a national crisis and the Space Race. While it carried no scientific sensors, its simple 'beep-beep-beep' radio signal could be heard by anyone with a shortwave radio. The signal lasted 22 days, providing accidental data about the Earth’s ionosphere. Interestingly, the 'star' most people reported seeing in the night sky wasn't the satellite at all; it was the massive 85-foot-long R-7 rocket booster that followed it into orbit. Sputnik's 96-minute laps around the globe proved the USSR could reach any point on Earth with a missile. Before burning up in January 1958, Sputnik 1 fundamentally changed the world, leading to the creation of NASA, the birth of GPS technology, and even the coining of the term 'beatnik.'
angle: Most people who claimed to see the first satellite in the night sky were actually looking at its massive, 85-foot discarded rocket booster.

claims.claim: Sputnik 1 was the world's first artificial Earth satellite.
It was launched by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957.
The satellite was approximately the size of a beach ball with a 58-centimeter diameter.
The satellite's name 'Sputnik' translates to 'traveling companion' or 'fellow traveler.'
Sputnik 1 completed one orbit of the Earth approximately every 96 to 98 minutes.
It emitted a distinctive 'beep-beep-beep' radio signal audible to shortwave radio operators.
The satellite was a highly polished metal sphere with four external antennas.
Sputnik 1's batteries lasted for 22 days before going dead on October 26, 1957.
The satellite burned up in the Earth's atmosphere on January 4, 1958.
The 85-foot-long core stage of the R-7 rocket also reached orbit and was more visible than the satellite itself.
The launch led directly to the creation of NASA in 1958.
The United States created the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA/DARPA) in response to the launch.
The satellite's signal allowed researchers to study the density of the ionosphere.
The U.S. attempt to launch the Vanguard TV3 satellite in December 1957 ended in a televised explosion.
The term 'beatnik' was coined by Herb Caen in 1958, inspired by the satellite's name.
The launch was part of the International Geophysical Year (IGY).
Monitoring the Doppler effect of Sputnik's signal led to the development of satellite navigation (GPS).

disputed: Whether pieces of Sputnik 1 survived re-entry and were found in California (S5 explores this as a claim by Bob Morgan, but S1 and S5 note that experts believe it burned up completely; the script should treat this as an unproven legend).

Visibility of the satellite (S1 states it was 6th magnitude and hard to see, while S3 suggests it might have been visible to the naked eye with perfect conditions; the script should emphasize the rocket booster was the primary object seen).

The level of surprise felt by the U.S. government (S1 says it was unanticipated, but S1 and S6 also state Eisenhower was forewarned by U-2 spy imagery; the script should attribute the 'shock' to the American public).
